#### Numerical Examples {#sec-pmc-531}

[**Numerical examples of matrix operations**]{#sec-pmc-531-intro}

Numerical examples of the matrix operations described on the [previous page](#sec-pmc-53) are given here to clarify these operations.

```{r}
#| label: setup-pmc-531
#| include: false
A <- matrix(c(5, 3, 6, 7), nrow = 2)
B <- matrix(c(3, 1, 2, 5), nrow = 2)
```

[**Sample matrices**]{#sec-pmc-531-sample}

If

$$
{\bf A} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 5 & 6 \\ 3 & 7
\end{array} \right] \,\,\,\,\,\,
\text{and} \,\,\,\,\,\,
{\bf B} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 5
\end{array} \right] \, ,
$$

then

[**Matrix addition, subtraction, and multiplication**]{#sec-pmc-531-arithmetic}

$$
{\bf A} + {\bf B} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 8 & 8 \\ 4 & 12
\end{array} \right] \,\,\,\,\,\,
\text{and} \,\,\,\,\,\,
{\bf A} - {\bf B} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 2
\end{array} \right]
$$

and

$$
{\bf AB} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 21 & 40 \\ 16 & 41
\end{array} \right] \,\,\,\,\,\,
\text{and} \,\,\,\,\,\,
{\bf BA} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 21 & 32 \\ 20 & 41
\end{array} \right] \, .
$$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-531-arithmetic
#| code-fold: true
A + B
A - B
A %*% B
B %*% A
```

[**Multiply matrix by a scalar**]{#sec-pmc-531-scalar}

To multiply a matrix by a given scalar, each element of the matrix is multiplied by that scalar

$$
2{\bf A} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 10 & 12 \\ 6 & 14
\end{array} \right] \,\,\,\,\,\,
\text{and} \,\,\,\,\,\,
0.5{\bf B} = \left[ \begin{array}{cc}
 1.5 & 1.0 \\ 0.5 & 2.5
\end{array} \right] \, .
$$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-531-scalar
#| code-fold: true
2 * A
0.5 * B
```

[**Pre-multiplying matrix by transpose of a vector**]{#sec-pmc-531-pre-multiply}

Pre-multiplying a $p \times n$ matrix by the transpose of a $p$-element vector yields a $n$-element transpose,

$$
{\bf c}^T = {\bf a}^T{\bf B} =
\left[ \begin{array}{cc} a_1 & a_2 \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}
b_{11} & b_{12} & b_{13} \\ b_{21} & b_{22} & b_{23}
\end{array} \right] =
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc} c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{array} \right] \, .
$$

[**Post-multiplying matrix by vector**]{#sec-pmc-531-post-multiply}

Post-multiplying a $p \times n$ matrix by an $n$-element vector yields an $n$-element vector,

$$
{\bf c} = {\bf Ba} =
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}
b_{11} & b_{12} & b_{13} \\ b_{21} & b_{22} & b_{23}
\end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c} a_1 \\ a_2 \\ a_3 \end{array} \right] =
\left[ \begin{array}{c} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{array} \right] \, .
$$

[**Quadratic form**]{#sec-pmc-531-quadratic}

It is not possible to pre-multiply a matrix by a column vector, nor to post-multiply a matrix by a row vector. The matrix product ${\bf a}^T{\bf Ba}$ yields a scalar and is called a quadratic form. Note that ${\bf B}$ must be a square matrix if ${\bf a}^T{\bf Ba}$ is to conform to multiplication. Here is an example of a quadratic form

$$
{\bf a}^T{\bf Ba} =
\left[ \begin{array}{cc} 2 & 3 \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{cc} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c} 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right] =
\left[ \begin{array}{cc} 11 & 7 \end{array} \right]
\left[ \begin{array}{c} 2 \\ 3 \end{array} \right] = 43 \, .
$$

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-531-quadratic
#| code-fold: true
a_vec <- c(2, 3)
B_quad <- matrix(c(1, 3, 2, 1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
t(a_vec) %*% B_quad %*% a_vec
```

[**Inverting a matrix**]{#sec-pmc-531-inverse}

The matrix analog of division involves an operation called *inverting a matrix.* Only square matrices can be inverted. Inversion is a tedious numerical procedure and it is best performed by computers. There are many ways to invert a matrix, but ultimately whichever method is selected by a program is immaterial. If you wish to try one method by hand, a very popular numerical method is the Gauss-Jordan method.

[**Identity matrix**]{#sec-pmc-531-identity}

To augment the notion of the inverse of a matrix, ${\bf A}^{-1}$ (${\bf A}$ inverse) we notice the following relation.

$$ {\bf A}^{-1}{\bf A} = {\bf A A}^{-1} = {\bf I} $$

where ${\bf I}$ is a matrix of form

$$ {\bf I} = \left[ \begin{array}{ccccc}
1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots &  & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1
\end{array} \right] \, . $$

${\bf I}$ is called the identity matrix and is a special case of a *diagonal* matrix. Any matrix that has zeros in all of the off-diagonal positions is a diagonal matrix.
